explanations.explanation: Yes, Herod, friend. Manaen had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch (Acts 13:1). He's listed right there with the prophets and teachers at Antioch. I think that's quite a background for one teacher.

Philip is a fair try, but the text doesn't say that here. Acts 13:1 says Manaen had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch. A tetrarch was a ruler over one part of a region. Philip isn't named in this verse.

Lysanias, now that's a name that came out of nowhere, friend. Nice reach, but Acts 13:1 says Manaen had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch. Lysanias isn't in this passage at all. I think that's one name that wandered in from another batch.

That's it. The Holy Spirit says, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” (Acts 13:2) Barnabas is the first name in the list and Saul is the last. The Spirit picked the two on the ends, and the three in the middle are still part of the team.

Simeon called Niger and Lucius of Cyrene are both on the list, friend, so you were close to the right list. But the Holy Spirit says, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” (Acts 13:2) Barnabas and Saul are the two named right there in the verse.

Lucius of Cyrene and Manaen are both listed with the prophets and teachers, but the Spirit didn't name them for this work. He says, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” (Acts 13:2) Barnabas and Saul are the two.

Yes, friend. After they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them off (Acts 13:3). Hands on Barnabas and Saul, and then off they went. I know a little about hands changing your day, because Mother Miller's hands once pulled me out of a 25-cent bin. Mine came with flour and a price sticker, though.

Oil is a reasonable guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. Acts 13:3 says they fasted and prayed, then laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul and sent them off. No oil gets mentioned at all. This sendoff is hands and prayer.

explanations.answer: They are given letters to carry
explanations.explanation: Letters would've been handy on a trip like this, but Acts 13:3 doesn't mention any. It says they fasted and prayed, laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul, and sent them off. That's the whole sendoff. I'd have packed a box of cookies, but that's me.

Cyprus is right. Barnabas and Saul went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus (Acts 13:4). That's an island, so there was no walking this one off. They went by boat, and the Holy Spirit sent them.
Crete is an island too, so your instinct was sound. But Acts 13:4 says they sailed from Seleucia to Cyprus. Crete isn't in this passage.
Malta is an island, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. Acts 13:4 says they sailed from Seleucia to Cyprus. Malta isn't in this passage at all.

Yes, friend. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues (Acts 13:5). A synagogue is a Jewish meeting place. That's where they started telling people God's word.

A marketplace would've had a crowd, I'll give you that. But Acts 13:5 says they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. A synagogue is a Jewish meeting place. Marketplaces aren't mentioned in this verse.

Courtyards sound like a nice, shady spot to talk, friend. But Acts 13:5 says they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. A synagogue is a Jewish meeting place. The verse doesn't mention courtyards.

explanations.answer: He wants to hear the word of God
explanations.explanation: Right on. The proconsul, a man of intelligence, summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God (Acts 13:7). Sergius Paulus is the proconsul, a Roman governor of the island. He sent for them because he wanted to listen.

explanations.answer: He wants them off his island
explanations.explanation: That would be a rude way to greet guests, friend. But Acts 13:7 says the proconsul summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God. He called them in to listen.

explanations.answer: He wants them put under arrest
explanations.explanation: Arrest is a dramatic guess, but it's not what happens here. Acts 13:7 says the proconsul summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God. He's a man of intelligence, and he wanted to listen.

explanations.answer: Turn the proconsul from the faith
explanations.explanation: That's it. Elymas opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith (Acts 13:8). Remember the proconsul is the one who summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God (Acts 13:7). Elymas is the one who opposed them.

explanations.answer: Get Barnabas and Saul thrown in prison
explanations.explanation: Prison would be a bigger move, friend, but the text doesn't say that. Acts 13:8 says Elymas opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith. His target was the proconsul, not a jail cell for Barnabas and Saul.

explanations.answer: Drive Barnabas and Saul off the island
explanations.explanation: Chasing them off the island makes sense as a plan, but that's not what the verse says. Acts 13:8 says Elymas opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith. His aim was the proconsul's belief.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, “…for a time you will be blind and unable to see the light of the sun.” (Acts 13:11) A time has a limit. Paul never says forever.

Correct, friend. Paul says, “…for a time you will be blind and unable to see the light of the sun.” (Acts 13:11) He says for a time, and not one word about forever. I think that matters, because a time is something that ends.

explanations.answer: He gropes around for someone to lead him
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, seeking someone to lead him by the hand (Acts 13:11). A man who just opposed them is now reaching around for a hand to hold. I think that's a hard moment to see.

explanations.answer: He begs Paul to take back his words
explanations.explanation: Begging is a natural thing to expect, friend, but the verse doesn't show it. Acts 13:11 says mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, seeking someone to lead him by the hand. Nothing in the text says he begged Paul for anything.

explanations.answer: He tries to run away from Paul
explanations.explanation: Running is a fair guess, but that's not what the verse says. Acts 13:11 says mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, seeking someone to lead him by the hand. He's reaching out, not bolting.

True, friend. When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord (Acts 13:12). He's the one who asked to hear God's word. In the end he believed.

Not this time, friend. Acts 13:12 says, “When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord.” He believed. The one who wanted to hear the word of God ended up believing it.
